prompt.context_jp: 行田の朝は、こはぜ屋の工房から始まる。
prompt.prompt_jp: 行田の朝___、こはぜ屋の工房から始まる。
prompt.prompt_en: Choose the particle that fits this opening narration.

feedback.correct_en: This is the opening line setting the scene — '(As for) Gyoda's mornings, they begin at Kohaze-ya.' は frames the morning as the known topic the narration is about to describe.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'Gyoda's morning' the newly-introduced subject that specifically starts there — like it was the answer to 'what begins at Kohaze-ya?', which does not match this scene-setting opener.

contrast_examples.jp: 行田の朝はこはぜ屋から始まる。
contrast_examples.en: Gyoda's mornings begin at Kohaze-ya. (topical description)

contrast_examples.jp: 行田の朝が、ついに来た。
contrast_examples.en: Gyoda's morning (finally) arrived. (new event announced)

prompt.context_jp: 足袋づくり百年の看板を掲げるこの町工場が、いま新しい靴に手を伸ばそうとしていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 足袋づくり百年の看板を掲げるこの町工場___、いま新しい靴に手を伸ばそうとしていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle introduces the factory as new information in this narration?

feedback.correct_en: The long modifier '100-year tabi-maker factory' freshly identifies this specific workshop to the reader. が presents it as newly-introduced information in a descriptive sentence.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark the factory as an already-established topic, but here the narrator is introducing it to us for the first time with a defining description.

contrast_examples.jp: 小さな町工場が、新しい靴に挑む。
contrast_examples.en: A small town factory takes on new shoes. (introducing)

contrast_examples.jp: その町工場は、足袋屋だ。
contrast_examples.en: That factory is a tabi maker. (already known topic)

prompt.context_jp: こはぜ屋の熱狂とは対照的に、実業団の練習場には冷ややかな空気が流れていた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 実業団の練習場には冷ややかな空気___流れていた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits the appearance of the atmosphere here?

feedback.correct_en: The chilly atmosphere is newly described sensory information in the scene. が presents it as something the narrator is pointing out as present.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would make 冷ややかな空気 the known topic, which doesn't fit — we're not comparing the chilly air with something; we're observing that it exists there.

contrast_examples.jp: 部屋に重い空気が流れていた。
contrast_examples.en: A heavy air hung in the room. (observed)

contrast_examples.jp: その空気は、やがて和らいだ。
contrast_examples.en: That atmosphere eventually softened. (known topic)

prompt.context_jp: 陸王という名は、この部屋ではまだ嘲笑の対象でしかない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 陸王という名___、この部屋ではまだ嘲笑の対象でしかない。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks the contrast implied here?

feedback.correct_en: は both topicalizes 'the name Rikuou' and signals contrast with other places — in Kohaze-ya it's celebrated, but in THIS room it is only mocked.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would make 'Rikuou' the exclusive new subject being identified, losing the implied contrast between settings that the narrator is building.

contrast_examples.jp: 陸王は、ここでは笑われている。
contrast_examples.en: Rikuou — here, it's laughed at. (contrastive topic)

contrast_examples.jp: 陸王が、まだ知られていない。
contrast_examples.en: It's Rikuou that isn't known yet. (new info)

prompt.context_jp: 小さな町工場の主が世界を口にした瞬間、店の空気は静かに張り詰めた。
prompt.prompt_jp: 小さな町工場の主___世界を口にした瞬間、店の空気は静かに張り詰めた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits in the subordinate 'the moment X said...' clause?

feedback.correct_en: Inside a '〜瞬間' relative/subordinate clause the subject typically takes が. It describes the specific event that triggered the shift in atmosphere.
feedback.incorrect_en: は generally doesn't appear as the subject particle inside tight relative/subordinate clauses like 〜瞬間; using it here would sound like you're starting a new main-clause topic.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が入ってきた瞬間、静まった。
contrast_examples.en: The moment he came in, it went quiet.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼は、入ってきたとき笑っていた。
contrast_examples.en: He, when he came in, was smiling. (topic set outside)

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢の声はグラウンドの端まで届いたが、監督はふりむこうともしない。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢の声はグラウンドの端まで届いたが、監督___ふりむこうともしない。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle best captures the contrast with Miyazawa's voice reaching?

feedback.correct_en: The sentence contrasts two things: Miyazawa's voice DID reach, but the coach (by contrast) won't even turn around. は on 監督 picks him out contrastively against the voice.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would just newly introduce the coach as subject, erasing the deliberate 'voice reached / coach ignores' contrast the narrator is building.

contrast_examples.jp: 声は届いたが、彼は答えない。
contrast_examples.en: The voice reached, but he doesn't answer. (contrast)

contrast_examples.jp: 声が届いたとき、彼が振り返った。
contrast_examples.en: When the voice reached, he turned around. (plain event)

prompt.context_jp: 顧客となる選手の足型を 業界で最も多く持ってんのが 村野さんです
prompt.prompt_jp: 業界で最も多く持ってんの___村野さんです。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 'the one who has the most' as exhaustive identification?

feedback.correct_en: This is the classic exhaustive-listing / 'the X is Y' pattern: 'The one who has the most molds in the industry is Mr. Murano.' が identifies Murano as THE answer.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would turn it into a general comment about 'the one with the most molds,' losing the pointed identification that answers 'who is it?'

contrast_examples.jp: 一番強いのが、彼です。
contrast_examples.en: The strongest one is him. (exhaustive)

contrast_examples.jp: 一番強いのは、努力した人です。
contrast_examples.en: The strongest, (generally,) is someone who worked hard.

prompt.context_jp: 小原は自慢げに腕組みし、その傍らで村野だけが黙って選手の足元を見つめている。
prompt.prompt_jp: その傍らで村野だけ___黙って選手の足元を見つめている。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits 'only Murano' as the single exception?

feedback.correct_en: だけが picks Murano out exclusively: everyone else celebrates, but he alone is silently watching the feet. Exhaustive listing of the sole exception.
feedback.incorrect_en: だけは would read as 'at least Murano' — a contrastive 'as for only him' topic. The narrative here is picking him out from the group, which is だけが's job.

contrast_examples.jp: 村野だけが疑っていた。
contrast_examples.en: Only Murano had doubts. (sole one)

contrast_examples.jp: 村野だけは信じていた。
contrast_examples.en: Murano, at least, believed. (contrastive)

prompt.context_jp: 「ああ… 少し ソールの減りが早いな」
prompt.prompt_jp: 少し ソールの減り___早いな。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Murano's observation about the sole?

feedback.correct_en: Murano is noticing something fresh — 'the wear is quick.' が introduces 減り as newly observed information, typical of describing a feature or state you just noticed.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would imply 減り was already an established topic being commented on, not something freshly observed on inspecting the shoe.

contrast_examples.jp: 靴の減りが早いな。
contrast_examples.en: The wear is fast, huh. (noticing)

contrast_examples.jp: 靴の減りは、仕方ない。
contrast_examples.en: As for shoe wear, it can't be helped. (general topic)

prompt.context_jp: こはぜ屋の面々は防寒具を握りしめ、選手たちのアップを食い入るように見つめていた。冷たい風がスタンドを吹き抜けていく。
prompt.prompt_jp: 冷たい風___スタンドを吹き抜けていく。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits for a vivid descriptive sentence of wind?

feedback.correct_en: Weather/nature descriptions like this are classic が-sentences: 風が吹く presents the wind as a fresh sensory event in the scene.
feedback.incorrect_en: 風は would turn 'cold wind' into a known topic you're commenting on, which doesn't fit a scenic insert that's just showing us what's happening.

contrast_examples.jp: 雨が降ってきた。
contrast_examples.en: It started to rain. (event)

contrast_examples.jp: この地方は、雨が多い。
contrast_examples.en: This region has a lot of rain. (topic)

prompt.context_jp: 直線に入りかけたその瞬間、茂木の足がふっと重心を失った。
prompt.prompt_jp: その瞬間、茂木の足___ふっと重心を失った。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits for the sudden event in a 瞬間 clause?

feedback.correct_en: A sudden, dramatic event — Mogi's leg losing balance — is presented as new information in the climax. が highlights the subject of this unexpected event.
feedback.incorrect_en: は would mark 茂木の足 as a known topic you're commenting on in general, which drains the suddenness and surprise.

contrast_examples.jp: 突然、彼の足が止まった。
contrast_examples.en: Suddenly, his leg stopped. (event)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼の足は、もう治っていた。
contrast_examples.en: His leg had already healed. (topic/state)

prompt.context_jp: 誰もが胸のどこかで、この一杯の後に控える戦いを察している。
prompt.prompt_jp: 誰___胸のどこかで、この一杯の後に控える戦いを察している。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle completes 'everyone' here?

feedback.correct_en: 誰もが is the fixed form meaning 'everyone (without exception).' It behaves like exhaustive-listing が — asserting every single person is included as subject.
feedback.incorrect_en: 誰もは is ungrammatical here; 誰も normally pairs with が in affirmative sentences, or appears alone with a negative predicate ('nobody').

contrast_examples.jp: 誰もが知っている。
contrast_examples.en: Everyone knows it.

contrast_examples.jp: 誰も知らない。
contrast_examples.en: Nobody knows it. (with negative)

prompt.context_jp: 茜が言葉を続ける前に、宮沢と大地は互いに視線を交わす。
prompt.prompt_jp: 茜が言葉を続ける前に、宮沢と大地___互いに視線を交わす。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle marks 'Miyazawa and Daichi' in this main clause?

feedback.correct_en: The subordinate clause already uses 茜が as the newly introduced subject. The main clause pivots to Miyazawa and Daichi as the established topic reacting — は is the natural main-clause topic marker.
feedback.incorrect_en: Using が again would make the father-son pair sound like newly introduced subjects, when the sentence structure clearly contrasts Akane's action vs. the two men's reaction.

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が話す前に、私は立ち上がった。
contrast_examples.en: Before he spoke, I stood up. (subordinate が + main は)

contrast_examples.jp: 彼が話した時、私が答えた。
contrast_examples.en: When he spoke, I answered. (two events, both が)

prompt.context_jp: 「アトランティスも落ちたな」
prompt.prompt_jp: アトランティス___落ちたな。
prompt.prompt_en: Which particle fits Murano's parting line about Atlantis?

feedback.correct_en: も adds 'Atlantis, too, has fallen,' implying it has joined other companies / situations that have declined. It's a resigned comparative judgment.
feedback.incorrect_en: が would merely state 'Atlantis fell' as new information, losing the bitter 'even Atlantis has sunk to this' nuance.

contrast_examples.jp: この会社も終わったな。
contrast_examples.en: This company, too, is finished.

contrast_examples.jp: 会社がつぶれた。
contrast_examples.en: The company went under. (plain)

prompt.context_jp: この場所で門前払いを食うのはもう何度目か、宮沢は靴底で土を確かめ、___を決めて歩み寄った。
prompt.prompt_jp: 宮沢は靴底で土を確かめ、___を決めて歩み寄った。
prompt.prompt_en: Which noun collocates with を決めて here to mean 'steeling himself'?

feedback.correct_en: 覚悟を決める is the set phrase meaning 'to brace yourself / commit mentally.' It fits Miyazawa's determination to face another rejection.
feedback.incorrect_en: 予定を決める means 'to set a schedule,' and 気持ちを決める isn't a natural fixed phrase; neither captures the resolve-steeling nuance.

contrast_examples.jp: 覚悟を決めて交渉に臨む。
contrast_examples.en: Steel oneself and go into negotiations.

contrast_examples.jp: 予定を決めてから出かける。
contrast_examples.en: Decide the schedule, then leave.

prompt.context_jp: この場所で門前払いを食うのはもう何度目か、宮沢は靴底で土を確かめ、覚悟を決めて歩み寄った。
prompt.prompt_jp: この場所で___を食うのはもう何度目か。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes the idiom meaning 'being turned away at the door'?

feedback.correct_en: 門前払いを食う literally 'eat a shut-door-at-the-gate' — the idiom for being turned away without a meeting. Perfect for Miyazawa's repeated rejections at the practice ground.
feedback.incorrect_en: 肩透かしを食う means 'to be dodged / let down' (a different nuance), and 門松 is a New Year's decoration — unrelated.

contrast_examples.jp: 営業先で門前払いを食った。
contrast_examples.en: I got turned away at the client's door.

contrast_examples.jp: 期待していたのに肩透かしを食った。
contrast_examples.en: I had hopes, but got brushed off.

prompt.context_jp: 彼が口にした一言が、上役の逆鱗に触れたところだった。
prompt.prompt_jp: 彼の一言が、上役の___に触れた。
prompt.prompt_en: Which noun completes the idiom for 'provoking a superior's wrath'?

feedback.correct_en: 逆鱗に触れる — 'to touch the inverted scale (of a dragon)' — is the idiom for setting off a superior's fury. Matches the coach's reaction to Mogi's remark.
feedback.incorrect_en: 琴線に触れる means 'to touch one's heartstrings' (positive emotion), the opposite feel. 心臓に触れる isn't an idiom at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 一言が社長の逆鱗に触れた。
contrast_examples.en: One word set off the boss's fury.

contrast_examples.jp: その言葉は心の琴線に触れた。
contrast_examples.en: The words touched my heartstrings. (moved me)

prompt.context_jp: 「せっかく こういう 盛り上がってる場なのに 水差すんじゃないよ」
prompt.prompt_jp: 盛り上がってる場なのに ___差すんじゃないよ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which noun completes the idiom for 'spoiling the mood'?

feedback.correct_en: 水を差す literally 'pour water on' — the idiom for throwing cold water on a mood or situation. Miyazawa is scolding Tomishima for killing the celebratory vibe.
feedback.incorrect_en: 塩を差す is not an idiom. 油を差す does exist but means literally 'to oil (machinery)' — unrelated to spoiling moods.

contrast_examples.jp: 二人の仲に水を差すな。
contrast_examples.en: Don't throw cold water on their relationship.

contrast_examples.jp: 機械に油を差す。
contrast_examples.en: Oil the machine. (literal)

prompt.context_jp: 「なかなか 一筋縄にはいかねえな」
prompt.prompt_jp: なかなか ___にはいかねえな。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrase completes the idiom 'won't go simply'?

feedback.correct_en: 一筋縄ではいかない is the set phrase meaning 'can't be handled by ordinary means / isn't straightforward.' Miyazawa is admitting the Rikuoh project is anything but simple.
feedback.incorrect_en: 一直線 and 一本道 both suggest 'straight line / single path' but neither pairs with にはいかない as a fixed idiom with this nuance.

contrast_examples.jp: この相手は一筋縄ではいかない。
contrast_examples.en: This opponent is a tough nut.

contrast_examples.jp: ゴールまで一直線だ。
contrast_examples.en: A straight shot to the goal.

prompt.context_jp: 「そんなの リップサービスに決まってるだろ」
prompt.prompt_jp: そんなの ___に決まってるだろ。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word matches the coach's dismissive meaning of 'empty flattery'?

feedback.correct_en: リップサービス in Japanese means 'lip service / empty words meant to please,' which fits the coach's cynical dismissal of Mogi's polite comment.
feedback.incorrect_en: セールストーク is a sales pitch, and キャッチコピー is an ad tagline — both describe commercial language, not polite social fluff.

contrast_examples.jp: ただのリップサービスだよ。
contrast_examples.en: That's just lip service.

contrast_examples.jp: うまいセールストークにのせられた。
contrast_examples.en: I got taken in by a slick sales pitch.

prompt.context_jp: 「お前の目は節穴か」
prompt.prompt_jp: お前の目は___か。
prompt.prompt_en: Which word completes the idiom 'are your eyes blind?'

feedback.correct_en: 目は節穴か ('are your eyes knot-holes?') is the sharp idiom for 'can't you see what's obvious?' Obara is harshly scolding Sayama for missing what the trial really revealed.
feedback.incorrect_en: 目は飾りか exists colloquially but is much weaker/different; 目は鏡か is not a fixed expression. 節穴 is the canonical form.

contrast_examples.jp: お前の目は節穴か。
contrast_examples.en: Are your eyes just knot-holes?! (strong rebuke)

contrast_examples.jp: 目は口ほどに物を言う。
contrast_examples.en: The eyes say as much as the mouth.

prompt.context_jp: 「前回のものより耐久性のある ソールの開発に成功したんです」
prompt.prompt_jp: 耐久性のあるソールの開発に___したんです。
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb collocates naturally with 開発に here?

feedback.correct_en: 開発に成功する — 'succeed in development' — is the standard business/technical collocation. Miyazawa is formally reporting a successful R&D outcome.
feedback.incorrect_en: 合格 (pass an exam) and 勝利 (victory in competition) both involve 'winning,' but neither collocates with 開発 for successful R&D.

contrast_examples.jp: 新素材の開発に成功した。
contrast_examples.en: Succeeded in developing a new material.

contrast_examples.jp: 試験に合格した。
contrast_examples.en: Passed the exam.

prompt.context_jp: 「では 改めまして シルクレイ完成を祝して 乾杯！」
prompt.prompt_jp: シルクレイ完成を___ 乾杯！
prompt.prompt_en: Which verb form completes the toast phrase?

feedback.correct_en: 〜を祝して is the semi-formal set phrase used in toasts: 'In celebration of X, cheers!' It's the standard register for 乾杯 openings.
feedback.incorrect_en: 喜んで ('gladly') doesn't take an object this way, and 祝って is grammatical but less idiomatic in formal toast speech — 祝して is the fixed toast collocation.

contrast_examples.jp: ご結婚を祝して、乾杯！
contrast_examples.en: In celebration of your marriage, cheers!

contrast_examples.jp: 喜んでお手伝いします。
contrast_examples.en: I'll gladly help.

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢がシルクレイ完成の夜に仲間へ語りかけた一言。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds most natural for Miyazawa's heartfelt 'I want to dream big'?

choices.text: みんな いてくれるからさ でかい夢 見たいんだよ
でかい夢を見るためにみんなを使いたい
みんなのおかげでかい夢見れる

feedback.correct_en: Option A matches the warm, inclusive casual register Miyazawa uses — 'because you're all here, I want to dream big.' からさ softens it collegially.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses 使いたい ('want to use'), which sounds cold/transactional and insults the team. C is ungrammatical (missing で: 'おかげで でかい夢').

contrast_examples.jp: みんながいるから頑張れる。
contrast_examples.en: I can push on because you're all here.

contrast_examples.jp: みんなを使って成功したい。
contrast_examples.en: I want to succeed by using everyone. (cold)

prompt.context_jp: 家族に陸王開発の進み具合を聞かれた宮沢の返事。
prompt.prompt_en: Which answer sounds most natural as a casual, honest 'it's not easy'?

choices.text: なかなか 一筋縄にはいかねえな
全然 一筋縄が行かないよ

feedback.correct_en: 一筋縄にはいかない is the fixed idiomatic form; なかなか adds the natural 'quite tricky' hedge. The casual ending ねえな fits Miyazawa's register.
feedback.incorrect_en: B and C break the idiom's structure (一筋縄 pairs with にはいかない, not が + 行く/ダメ). Native speakers would hear them as broken.

contrast_examples.jp: この件はなかなか一筋縄にはいかない。
contrast_examples.en: This matter isn't straightforward at all.

contrast_examples.jp: 交渉は一筋縄ではいかなかった。
contrast_examples.en: The negotiation wasn't simple.

prompt.context_jp: 村野が自分のシューフィッター哲学を宮沢に語る場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing best matches Murano's reflective, professional tone?

choices.text: その選手と同じ夢を見ることが シューフィッターの仕事だと 私は そう思っています
選手と夢見るのがシューフィッターの仕事だと思うぞ
選手の夢を見るのが靴屋の仕事じゃない？

feedback.correct_en: A keeps Murano's calm, polite 〜と思っています register and the key phrase 同じ夢を見る (share the same dream). It fits his quietly principled voice.
feedback.incorrect_en: B uses blunt ぞ and drops 同じ, sounding macho and off-character. C's phrasing 選手の夢を見る means 'dream ABOUT the athlete' — a different meaning entirely.

contrast_examples.jp: 選手と同じ夢を見る。
contrast_examples.en: Share the same dream as the athlete.

contrast_examples.jp: 選手の夢を見る。
contrast_examples.en: Have a dream about the athlete. (different!)

prompt.context_jp: 宮沢が有村に挨拶する場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which greeting sounds most natural when thanking someone for making time for you?

choices.text: 今日は すいません お時間いただいて
今日は 時間をあげてくれて ありがとう
今日は 時間が欲しいです

feedback.correct_en: お時間いただいて is standard polite business language for 'thanks for giving me your time.' すいません softens it humbly — just right for a small-factory owner addressing a producer.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's 時間をあげてくれて uses あげる wrongly (sounds like 'you gave time to someone'); C just states 'I want time,' which is a request, not a thank-you.

contrast_examples.jp: お時間いただいてすみません。
contrast_examples.en: Sorry for taking your time. (polite thanks)

contrast_examples.jp: 少しお時間いただけますか。
contrast_examples.en: Could I have a bit of your time? (request)

prompt.context_jp: 村野が茂木の靴の状態を見抜いて指摘する場面。
prompt.prompt_en: Which phrasing sounds most natural for 'the shoes aren't clicking with you'?

choices.text: 本当は しっくりきてないんじゃないか？
本当は 合わさってないでしょう？
本当は フィットじゃないか？

feedback.correct_en: しっくりくる means 'to feel right / click,' and the negative しっくりきてない is the natural idiomatic way to say shoes don't feel right. 〜んじゃないか softens it as a gentle guess.
feedback.incorrect_en: B's 合わさってない means '(two things) aren't joined,' wrong semantics. C's フィットじゃないか is Japanglish — フィット as a bare noun doesn't work this way; you'd need フィットしていない.

contrast_examples.jp: この靴、しっくりこないな。
contrast_examples.en: These shoes don't feel quite right.

contrast_examples.jp: この靴、ちゃんとフィットしていない。
contrast_examples.en: These shoes don't fit properly.
